name: Diarrhea
preview_text: Not all diarrhea is the same. The acute, foul-smelling, urgent kind after a heavy meal is a very different pattern from the chronic, watery, early-morning kind that leaves you cold...

conventional_description:
Diarrhea is defined as the passage of three or more loose or watery stools per day. Acute diarrhea often results from viral or bacterial infections, food poisoning, or medication side effects, and typically resolves within a few days. Chronic diarrhea, lasting more than four weeks, may signal an underlying condition such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), celiac disease, or malabsorption disorders.
Diagnosis usually involves a medical history, stool tests, and sometimes blood work, endoscopy, or imaging. Treatment focuses on rehydration, dietary adjustments, and addressing the underlying cause - but many people still struggle with recurring episodes when no clear medical explanation is found.
conventional_treatments: Standard care centers on preventing dehydration with oral rehydration solutions and, when needed, using antidiarrheal medications like loperamide. Antibiotics may be prescribed if a bacterial infection is confirmed. For chronic conditions, management includes dietary modifications (low FODMAP, gluten-free), probiotics, and medications that target the underlying disease, such as anti-inflammatories for IBD or bile acid binders for bile acid diarrhea.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the Spleen is the central organ of digestion, responsible for transforming food into Qi and separating the clear fluids from the turbid waste. When the Spleen is strong, it sends the clear upward and the turbid downward in an orderly way.
Diarrhea happens when this process breaks down - either because the Spleen is too weak to hold the clear up, or because a pathogenic factor like Dampness, Heat, or Cold is obstructing its work and forcing fluids downward prematurely.
But the Spleen doesn't work alone. The Kidney provides the foundational Yang warmth that fuels the Spleen's digestive fire - when Kidney Yang is weak, the whole system runs cold and watery stools with undigested food are common, especially at dawn.
The Liver, when stressed, can surge sideways and attack the Spleen, causing sudden, cramping diarrhea that flares with emotional upset. Even the Large Intestine can be directly invaded by Damp-Heat or Cold-Damp from contaminated food or weather, producing acute, urgent episodes.
This is why TCM never treats all diarrhea the same way. An acute, foul-smelling, burning diarrhea after eating spicy food points to Damp-Heat in the Large Intestine. A chronic, loose stool with bloating and fatigue after meals signals Spleen Qi Deficiency.
An early-morning watery stool with cold limbs and a sore back reveals Kidney and Spleen Yang Deficiency. Each pattern has its own internal logic, its own tongue and pulse signs, and its own specific herbal formula and acupuncture protocol.
classical_translation: "When dampness prevails, there will be sloppy diarrhea. This early text identifies dampness as the primary pathogenic factor in diarrhea, a principle that remains central to TCM diagnosis and treatment today."

tcm_diagnosis:
Acute watery diarrhea with abdominal pain that feels better with warmth and a heavy, sluggish sensation points to Cold‑Damp invading the Spleen. The tongue usually looks pale with a thick white coating, and the pulse feels slow and soft. This pattern often follows exposure to cold, damp weather or eating too many raw, cold foods.
When diarrhea is urgent, yellow, sticky, and foul‑smelling with a burning sensation around the anus, Damp‑Heat in the Large Intestine is the likely culprit. The tongue is red with a yellow, greasy coating, and the pulse is rapid and slippery. This often flares after eating contaminated or spicy, greasy food.
Chronic, on‑and‑off loose stools with fatigue, poor appetite, and bloating after meals suggest Spleen Qi Deficiency. The tongue is pale and swollen with teeth marks, and the pulse is weak. When these signs are joined by cold limbs, watery stools with undigested food, and a strong dislike of cold, the pattern has deepened into Spleen Yang Deficiency.
Diarrhea triggered by emotional stress, with cramping pain and a sense of fullness in the chest and sides, indicates Rebellious Liver Qi invading the Spleen. The tongue may look normal or slightly pale, but the pulse feels wiry, especially on the left side. This pattern often alternates with constipation and worsens with mood swings.

patterns.symptoms: ["Loose stools or watery diarrhea, often with undigested food", "Worse after eating, especially large or heavy meals", "Persistent fatigue and lack of energy", "Poor appetite with abdominal bloating", "Dull, pale complexion", "Heaviness or weakness in the limbs"]
patterns.worse_with: Raw, cold, or iced foods and drinks, Overeating or heavy, greasy meals, Overexertion and chronic fatigue, Excessive worry or overthinking
patterns.better_with: Warm, cooked, simple meals, Rest after eating, Warmth on the abdomen
patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen is the engine of digestion, transforming food into Qi and separating clear fluids from turbid waste. When Spleen Qi is weak, it can no longer hold this upward, separating movement, so moisture and partially digested food slip downward into the intestines. This produces chronic loose stools or watery diarrhea that often worsens right after eating, because the Spleen is immediately overwhelmed by the meal.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale, puffy body with tooth marks and a thin white coating. Pulse: Weak and soft overall, especially at the right middle (Guan) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spleen Qi is like a digestive fire that transforms food. Raw, cold, and heavy foods dampen that fire, while warm, cooked meals and rest give it the gentle, steady fuel it needs. Overthinking and worry directly knot the Spleen Qi, and physical exhaustion depletes it further, so calming the mind and conserving energy are essential to healing.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods like rice congee, well-cooked vegetables, and small amounts of lean protein. Avoid raw, cold, greasy, dairy, and sugary foods that burden the Spleen. Eat smaller, more frequent meals and rest briefly after eating. Gentle daily movement like walking supports Qi flow, but avoid exhaustion.

patterns.better_with: Bland, easily digestible foods like congee, Cooling foods such as cucumber and watermelon, Drinking warm water or barley water, Rest in a cool environment, Light physical activity like walking
patterns.why_this_happens: Damp-Heat is a heavy, sticky, and hot pathogenic mixture that can accumulate in the Large Intestine, often after eating contaminated or greasy food, or during hot, humid weather. The Heat irritates the intestinal lining, causing urgency and a burning sensation, while the Dampness makes the stools sticky and difficult to pass completely. Together, they disrupt the normal downward movement of waste, leading to frequent, foul-smelling diarrhea that feels hot and incomplete.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a thick, yellow, greasy coating, thickest in the centre and root. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and rapid (数 shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work:
Greasy and spicy foods directly generate Dampness and Heat in the body, which pour down into the intestines and worsen the diarrhea. Alcohol and coffee are warming and add to the Heat, while hot, humid weather introduces external Damp-Heat that can trigger an episode. Emotional stress stirs up internal Heat and can aggravate the condition.
In contrast, bland, cooling foods help to clear Heat and drain Dampness without overburdening the digestive system. Barley water and mung bean soup are traditional remedies that gently leach out Dampness and cool the body. Rest allows the body's resources to focus on clearing the pathogen, and a cool environment prevents further accumulation of Heat.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Stick to a bland, easily digestible diet: congee, steamed vegetables, and lean protein. Avoid all greasy, fried, spicy, and heavily seasoned foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which feed Damp-Heat. Drink plenty of warm water, and consider barley water or mung bean soup to help clear Heat and Dampness. Rest in a cool, well-ventilated space until the acute phase passes.

patterns.why_this_happens: When cold and dampness from the environment or diet invade the body, they settle in the Spleen and Stomach. Cold contracts and slows movement, while dampness is heavy and sticky, together obstructing the Spleen's ability to transform food and separate clear from turbid. The Spleen fails to send the pure upward, so fluids and undigested food rush downward, causing watery diarrhea. The cold also congeals Qi in the abdomen, leading to dull pain that feels better with warmth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks; thick white greasy coating, excessively moist. Pulse: soggy (Ru) or slippery (Hua) and slow (Chi).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and dampness are the direct causes of this pattern. Cold constricts and slows the Spleen's function, while dampness creates heaviness and loose stools. Warmth and drying measures counteract both: heat relaxes the congealed Qi and eases pain, while warm, dry foods and herbs help the Spleen transform dampness. Ingesting more cold or damp substances adds to the burden, making diarrhea and heaviness worse.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the abdomen warm and avoid damp, cold environments. Eat small, frequent meals of warm, easily digested foods like rice congee with a little fresh ginger. Strictly avoid raw, cold, greasy, and dairy foods until stools are formed. Sipping warm ginger tea throughout the day helps warm the middle and dispel cold-damp.

patterns.worse_with: Cold or raw foods and drinks, Overeating or heavy, greasy meals, Cold, damp weather, Physical overexertion
patterns.better_with: Warmth on the belly, Warm, cooked meals, Rest and lying down, Gentle pressure on the abdomen
patterns.why_this_happens: Your Spleen is the body's digestive furnace. When its Yang energy is weak, the furnace runs cold. It can no longer fully cook and separate food, so watery stools rush out, often carrying undigested bits. This cold deficiency also fails to warm the belly and limbs, leaving you craving heat and prone to chills.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale, puffy, and tender with teeth marks on the edges and a white, slippery coating. Pulse: Deep, slow, and weak - especially soft at the right wrist’s middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spleen Yang is the digestive fire. Cold and raw foods douse that fire, making the Spleen too weak to separate fluids and food, so diarrhea worsens. Warmth, rest, and easily digested foods conserve the little Yang you have, allowing the Spleen to slowly rebuild its cooking power and firm up the stools.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat only warm, well-cooked foods like congee, soups, and stews. Generously use ginger, cinnamon, and a pinch of black pepper. Avoid all raw, cold, and frozen items, as well as dairy and greasy foods. A warm compress or moxa stick over the belly button each morning can make a big difference.

patterns.why_this_happens: When you overeat or eat too many rich, greasy foods, your Stomach simply cannot process the load. The undigested food sits and ferments, creating a turbid, sour mass. This stagnation disrupts the normal downward movement of Qi, causing foul-smelling, rotten-egg-like diarrhea as the body tries to expel the waste.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal body with a thick, greasy coating, thickest in the centre. Pulse: slippery (滑, huá) and full, especially at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overeating or rich food directly overwhelms the Stomach, creating the very stagnation that causes this type of diarrhea. Passing stool or gas physically relieves the internal pressure and turbidity. Light, bland food gives the digestive system a rest, allowing the Stomach Qi to recover its downward movement naturally.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, simple meals of congee or well-cooked vegetables until your appetite returns. Avoid all greasy, fried, dairy, and raw foods for a few days. Chew slowly and stop eating before you feel full.

patterns.pattern_name: Rebellious Liver Qi invading the Spleen
patterns.symptoms: ["Cramping abdominal pain before diarrhea", "Pain relief after bowel movement", "Diarrhea triggered by stress or anger", "Distension and fullness along the ribs", "Irritability, frequent sighing", "Alternating constipation and loose stools"]
patterns.worse_with: Stress or anger, Raw or cold foods, Irregular eating, Overeating, Fatigue
patterns.better_with: Emotional calm, Warm compress on abdomen, Small frequent meals, Gentle walking
patterns.why_this_happens: When stress, frustration, or anger are not expressed healthily, the Liver’s Qi can become stuck and then surge sideways, attacking the Spleen. The Spleen is responsible for transforming food and fluids, and this attack disrupts its ability to hold things together, causing an urgent, cramping diarrhea. The pain often builds before the bowel movement and eases once the tension is released.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly pale, possible teeth marks, thin white coating. Pulse: wiry overall, with the left guan position distinctly wiry and the right guan soft.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and anger directly cause Liver Qi to surge and attack the Spleen, so emotional calm prevents the very mechanism of this diarrhea. Warmth and small, cooked meals support the Spleen's digestive fire, while raw, cold, or heavy foods weaken it further. Gentle movement helps unstick stagnant Liver Qi, and rest restores the Spleen's energy.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods and avoid raw, cold, or greasy items that tax the Spleen. Eat small, regular meals and chew thoroughly. Practice stress management like gentle walking, tai chi, or meditation to keep Liver Qi flowing smoothly.

patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Yang is the body's foundational warmth, like a pilot light that fuels the Spleen's digestive fire. When it weakens, the Spleen can no longer "cook" food properly, leading to undigested food passing straight through as loose stools. The hallmark early-morning diarrhea (around 5 AM) happens because Yang Qi is at its lowest ebb just before dawn, so the body dumps cold water and undigested matter.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Pale, swollen, puffy tongue body with teeth marks and a white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, weak, and slow, especially feeble at the Chi (rear) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is the body's foundational warmth, like the pilot light for the Spleen's digestive fire. Cold, raw foods, and exhaustion drain that fire, leaving the Spleen unable to cook food, which leads to undigested stools and early morning diarrhea. Warmth, rest, and warming foods gently stoke the fire, allowing the Spleen to transform food properly and stop the diarrhea.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat only warm, cooked foods; avoid raw, cold, and iced items completely. Add gentle warming spices like ginger, cinnamon, and black pepper to meals. Keep the abdomen and lower back warm at all times, and consider moxibustion on the lower back and navel area. Rest adequately and avoid overwork.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with acute diarrhea from food poisoning?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acute diarrhea from contaminated food often falls under the Damp-Heat or Food Stagnation patterns. Herbal formulas that clear Heat, dry Dampness, and eliminate stagnation can shorten the course and relieve cramping and urgency. However, if you have a high fever, bloody stools, or signs of severe dehydration, seek urgent medical care first - TCM can then support recovery.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture effective for chronic diarrhea?
faqs.answer: Many patients with chronic loose stools or IBS-D find acupuncture very helpful, especially when combined with herbs. Points like Zusanli ST-36 and Tianshu ST-25 strengthen the Spleen and regulate the intestines. Treatment frequency is usually once or twice a week, and improvements in stool form and urgency are often felt within the first few weeks. Long-standing Spleen and Kidney deficiency patterns need more time, but acupuncture can gradually restore digestive resilience.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs with my prescription antidiarrheal medication?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, but you should inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor about everything you are taking. Some herbs have astringent or drying properties that could compound the effects of loperamide. If you are on medication for an underlying condition like IBD, your TCM practitioner will select herbs that support rather than interfere with your treatment. Never stop a prescribed medication abruptly without consulting your doctor.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet while taking TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a huge role. Across all patterns, TCM recommends avoiding raw, cold, and greasy foods, which burden the Spleen. Favor warm, cooked foods like congee and soups. Your practitioner will give specific advice based on your pattern - for example, if you have Damp-Heat, you'll avoid spicy and fried foods; if you have Cold-Damp, you'll emphasize warming foods like ginger. Dietary changes often speed up improvement dramatically.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results with TCM?
faqs.answer: Acute diarrhea often responds within a day or two of starting herbs. Chronic patterns take longer - you might notice less urgency and better-formed stools in 2-4 weeks, but full resolution of Spleen or Kidney deficiency can take 3-6 months of consistent treatment. The key is patience: TCM is rebuilding your digestive strength, not just stopping the symptom.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for children with diarrhea?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be very gentle and effective for children. Pediatric diarrhea is often due to Spleen weakness or food stagnation. Herbal doses are adjusted, and acupressure or pediatric tuina massage may be used instead of needles. Always work with a practitioner experienced in pediatrics, and seek urgent care if the child shows signs of dehydration, blood in stool, or lethargy.

faqs.question: Can stress really cause diarrhea, and can TCM help?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. The Liver-Spleen connection is well recognized in TCM: emotional stress constrains the Liver, which then attacks the Spleen, leading to sudden cramping and diarrhea. This is the Rebellious Liver Qi invading the Spleen pattern. Herbs like Bai Zhu and Bai Shao, along with acupuncture points such as Taichong LR-3, soothe the Liver and strengthen the Spleen. Many people find that as their stress response improves, the diarrhea becomes far less reactive.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine, Tongxieyaofang, alleviates diarrhea via gut microbiota remodeling: evidence from network pharmacology and full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing
research.description: This study combined network pharmacology and 16S rRNA sequencing to investigate how Tong Xie Yao Fang (TXYF) relieves diarrhea. The results indicated that TXYF significantly improved diarrhea symptoms by restoring gut microbiota balance, reducing inflammation, and repairing intestinal barrier function. The formula's multi-target action supports its traditional use for Liver-Spleen disharmony diarrhea.
research.periodical: Li J, Zhang Y, Wang X, et al. Chinese herbal medicine, Tongxieyaofang, alleviates diarrhea via gut microbiota remodeling: evidence from network pharmacology and full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Front Cell Infect Microbiol. 2024;14:1502373.

research.title: Acupuncture for irritable bowel syndrome
research.description: This Cochrane systematic review assessed acupuncture for IBS, including diarrhea-predominant subtypes. The review found that acupuncture may improve abdominal pain and bowel function compared to no treatment or sham acupuncture, though the evidence was not conclusive due to risk of bias. The authors called for larger, well-designed trials.
research.periodical: Manheimer E, Cheng K, Wieland LS, et al. Acupuncture for irritable bowel syndrome. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012;5:CD005111.
